title: Orbits
subtitle: Where the planets are, and why the seasons turn

children.html:
The planets go round the Sun on nearly circular paths, all in roughly the same plane. The inner four are small and rocky; the outer four are giants.

  • Mercury is the closest.
  • Neptune is the farthest.

children.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
children.why: Mercury orbits at about 0.39 AU, closer than any other planet.

children.html: An astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.
Pluto was counted as a planet until 2006.
The orbit of every planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one of the two foci.

The Earth's distance from the Sun barely changes over a year. Its axis, though, is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, and the tilt keeps pointing the same way as the Earth goes round.

For half the year the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun: its days are longer and the sunlight strikes it more steeply. For the other half the southern hemisphere does.

children.prompt: Explain why the Earth has seasons.
children.model: The Earth's axis is tilted. As the Earth orbits, each hemisphere in turn leans towards the Sun, getting longer days and more direct sunlight: that hemisphere's summer.
